There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette: Meet Hone, a 63-year-old Maori community organizer from New Zealand. His life took a dramatic turn three years ago when he was involved in a near-fatal car accident while driving home from a community meeting. The crash left him with physical scars and a lingering sense of dread that he couldn't shake off. Hone's memories of the accident are fragmented, like pieces of a puzzle he can't quite assemble. He recalls the sound of screeching tires, the feeling of weightlessness as his car spun out of control, and the eerie silence that followed. But there are gaping holes in his recollection - moments he knows occurred but are now shrouded in darkness. His inability to fill those gaps frustrates him, leaving him with a sense of disconnection from his own experience. As Hone navigates his daily life, certain triggers can transport him back to that fateful night. When someone expresses anger, even calmly, he feels his body tense up, ready to respond as if the threat is still imminent. The sight of military or police uniforms also unsettles him, reminding him of the authority figures who arrived at the crash scene. These encounters leave Hone feeling emotionally numb, as if a switch has been flipped and he's no longer fully present. What frightens Hone most is that these triggers seem to confirm his deepest fears - that he's still in danger, even when logic tells him otherwise. He's come to believe that his body is an unreliable ally, prone to reacting as if the threat is still real, even when it's just a memory. This sense of bodily betrayal reinforces his feelings of self-blame; Hone is convinced that the accident happened because of something he did or didn't do. These negative appraisals cast a long shadow over his memories of the event, making it harder for him to recall specifics without getting bogged down in guilt and anxiety. As Hone tries to make sense of his experience, his partial recollections feed back into his negative self-appraisals. He can't shake off the feeling that there's something he's missing, some crucial detail that would explain why this happened to him. This nagging uncertainty fuels his emotional numbness, making it harder for him to connect with others or find joy in activities he once loved. Hone's struggles have taken a toll on his relationships and work as a community organizer. His inability to fully engage with others has made it challenging to build trust and facilitate meaningful dialogue - essential skills for his role. He feels like an outsider, watching life unfold from behind a veil of numbness and fear. As he seeks help, Hone hopes to find a way to reconnect with himself and others, to learn how to live with the memories that haunt him without being consumed by them. Hone's journey toward healing is fraught with uncertainty, but it begins with acknowledging the web of negative appraisals, memories, and triggers that has entangled his life. By slowly untangling these threads, he may begin to find a way out of the darkness, back into a world where emotions are vivid and connections feel real.
